1.pericope_label: Woe be unto the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture
debates: Whether the opening word is an exclamation or a denunciation
Who the pastors are
Who the gathered remnant is
outliers: Calvin reads the three charges of the second verse as stated in inverted order, effect first and cause last
Ellicott finds in the verb for setting up an echo of the names of the two kings just condemned
themes: An honourable title conceded in order to be stripped away
Promise and threatening mixed in one oracle
Neglect counted as active scattering
An office not abolished because it has been abused

5.pericope_label: I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and this is his name whereby he shall be called
debates: Whether the name identifies the King with God
Whether the branch is one king or a whole line
What the days of this king means
outliers: Clarke believes Jesus to be Jehovah but denies that this text says so, and refuses to rest the doctrine on what he judges a dubious construction
Ellicott makes the identification and the imputed righteousness applications of the name rather than its direct meaning
themes: A sprout from a root rather than a branch from a trunk
A name read as a watchword rather than a predicate
A doctrine argued from a disputed clause
A reign measured by perpetuity rather than by years

7.pericope_label: They shall no more say, The LORD liveth which brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt
debates: What the opening particle means
Whether the promise has yet been accomplished
Why the older deliverance is set aside
outliers: Calvin holds that the secret working of providence on the minds of men accomplishes more than miracles that reverse the course of nature
Ellicott reports that the Greek version omits these verses here and inserts them at the end of the chapter
themes: A greater deliverance measured against a lesser
Exile claimed by God as his own act
The same hand that kills able to make alive
A hinge from the kings to the prophets

9.pericope_label: Mine heart within me is broken because of the prophets; for the land is full of adulterers
debates: Whether the opening words are a title or part of the sentence
Whether the adultery named is literal or spiritual
What the word rendered swearing means
outliers: Calvin says that zeal displayed where there is no need is mere apery, and that vehemence belongs only to disorder
Ellicott insists the adultery must be taken literally, against the reading Clarke gives
themes: A superscription mistaken for a clause
A prophet undone by his own message
Silence in teachers counted as complicity
Might exulted in where right was wanting

11.pericope_label: For both prophet and priest are profane; wherefore their way shall be unto them as slippery ways in the darkness
debates: Whether the verb of defiling is passive or transitive
Whether the darkness belongs to the slippery way or to the thrusting
What the mention of the house of God adds to the charge
outliers: Calvin holds that freedom to rebuke comes only from a clear conscience, so that the guilt of the prophets is the cause of their silence
Calvin rejects a rendering that separates the darkness from the slippery way as spoiling the force of the passage
themes: Silence explained by complicity
A charge doubled by the place where it was found
Prosperity that turns out to be slippery ground
A punishment deferred to an appointed year

13.pericope_label: I have seen folly in the prophets of Samaria, but in the prophets of Jerusalem an horrible thing
debates: What the word describing the prophets of Samaria means
Whether the last word of the fifteenth verse means pollution or profaneness
Whether the adulterers of the fourteenth verse are the prophets or the people
outliers: Calvin holds that the men who claimed to be the faithful ministers of God were by far the worst, so that by comparison the northern prophets could be called merely fatuous
Calvin says shame restrains men as fear does, so that removing shame is itself a strengthening of the wicked
themes: Guilt measured by comparison rather than by itself
A claim to speak for God counted worse than open idolatry
A table prepared that holds only poison
Pollution spreading outward from the place of worship

16.pericope_label: Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you; they make you vain
debates: Whether the participle at the seventeenth verse belongs to the preceding sentence
Whether the clause naming the despisers is spoken by God or reported from the prophets
What the word rendered imagination means
outliers: Ellicott finds the false prophets self-convicted by the very verb they used of the divine speech
Calvin says the word vision is conceded to them improperly, since they were only apes as prophets
themes: A sacred name conceded and then discredited
Comfort without repentance as the mark of a false teacher
A doubled verb read as boldness
Discernment promised to those who ask for it

18.pericope_label: For who hath stood in the counsel of the LORD? Behold, a whirlwind of the LORD is gone forth in fury
debates: Whose words the question at the eighteenth verse is
What kind of storm is meant
What is meant by the thoughts of his heart
outliers: Calvin says the usual reading of the eighteenth verse is mistaken and that the words are a taunt thrown by the false prophets at the true
Calvin reads the storm as pregnant and in travail, bursting on the head of the wicked
themes: A privy council no false prophet had entered
A storm named from the burning winds of the south
A heart that is a fixed purpose and not a change of mind
Judgment sent out like a messenger on an errand

21.pericope_label: I have not sent these prophets, yet they ran: am I a God at hand, and not a God afar off?
debates: Whether the fruit of a ministry is a test of its truth
How the questions about nearness and distance are to be taken
What proves a man sent
outliers: Calvin answers the argument from numbers by saying that if God is the author of his mission he is, though alone, superior to the whole world
Calvin charges the Greek translators with reversing the sense of the twenty-third verse
themes: A messenger who runs before he is sent
Results offered as the proof of a calling
A God imagined to be short-sighted
Hiding places that only deepen the judgment

25.pericope_label: I have heard what the prophets said, that prophesy lies in my name, saying, I have dreamed
debates: How the twenty-sixth verse is to be construed
Whether the clause speaks of the name of God or of his law
How a true dream may be distinguished from a false one
outliers: Calvin rejects three conjectural emendations of the twenty-sixth verse as unsupported by any manuscript or early version
Clarke lists four marks by which a true dream may be known
themes: A title claimed by both sides of a dispute
A channel of revelation discredited by misuse
Orthodox principles held alongside a false commission
A hidden defection counted more dangerous than an open one

28.pericope_label: What is the chaff to the wheat? Is not my word like as a fire, and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
debates: Whether the opening particle of the twenty-ninth verse should be read as a word for power
Whether the fire and the hammer describe the effect on the faithful or on the reprobate
Whom the command to tell a dream is addressed to
outliers: Clarke warns against supposing the scriptures sufficient of themselves without the Spirit, since fire must be applied and a hammer wielded
Clarke illustrates the hammer from the roasting of tin ore before it is crushed in a stamp mill
themes: Controversy taken as an excuse for indifference
A dream permitted so long as it is called a dream
One word that is food to some and poison to others
A fire that refines and a fire that devours

30.pericope_label: Behold, I am against the prophets that steal my words every one from his neighbour
debates: What the stealing of words means
Whether the tongue is smoothed or raised
What the word rendered lightness means
outliers: Calvin rejects the common reading of the thirty-first verse and takes the verb in its plain sense of raising the tongue
Ellicott quotes an English poet on a hollow eloquence poured out in one weak, washy, everlasting flood
themes: Borrowed phrases repeated among a clique
A tongue taken up as an instrument
An oracle formula turned back in irony
A commission as the only test of weight

33.pericope_label: What is the burden of the LORD? Ye shall mention the burden of the LORD no more
debates: Whether the phrase was used in mockery or in boastful assumption
Whether the word was a new coinage of the prophets
What the answer of the thirty-third verse means
outliers: Ellicott dissents from the common view and makes the phrase the boast of the false prophets rather than a jeer at Jeremiah
Henry defends the prophets against the charge of coining a new word, since the Spirit of God is not tied to our rules of speaking
themes: A word turned into a byword
Ridicule used to disarm a message
A burden its bearer will be relieved of
Bitterness in the word traced back to the hearer

37.pericope_label: Since ye say, The burden of the LORD, behold, I will utterly forget you, and I will forsake you
debates: What the verb at the thirty-ninth verse means
How far the everlasting reproach extends
Whether one phrase could deserve so heavy a sentence
outliers: Calvin proposes that a single word has been displaced in the text and offers a rendering on that supposition
Calvin limits the everlasting reproach in time, holding that the Church could not be doomed to a reproach without end
themes: A protest against solemn words gone hollow
A play on words carried into the sentence itself
A burden set down and not taken up again
A boast stripped away
